track.title: Accounting 301
track.summary: Financial statement analysis, earnings quality, unit economics, budgeting, forecasting, and decision use.

orientationEssays.title: Using accounting without being fooled by it
orientationEssays.plainLanguageSummary: Financial analysis uses accounting numbers to ask better questions. The goal is not to worship ratios, but to understand performance, risk, and truth quality.
orientationEssays.historicalOrigin: As capital markets and professional management grew, accounting records became tools for comparison, valuation, lending, budgeting, and fraud detection.
orientationEssays.socialImportance: Investors, employees, lenders, founders, and citizens rely on financial claims. Better analysis helps people see whether those claims are durable or distorted.
orientationEssays.whyLearnersCare: A college senior should be able to read statements, notice cash stress, understand margins, and ask competent follow-up questions.
commonObjections: Learners may think ratios automatically produce a decision.
Learners may assume audited accounting numbers are the same as economic truth.
deeperPaths: Compare two companies in the same industry using common-size statements.
Study real earnings-quality failures and the accounting choices behind them.

concepts.title: Statement Analysis
concepts.summary: Margins, liquidity, leverage, and returns help summarize performance, but only when interpreted in context.
objectives: Choose the right ratio family for a financial question.

diagnostics.prompt: Which ratio family is most directly about the ability to pay near-term obligations: liquidity, leverage, or margin?

practice.prompt: Which ratio family is most directly about debt burden: liquidity, leverage, or margin?
hints: Think about who has claims on the company besides owners.

feedback.correct: Correct. Leverage ratios describe debt and capital structure.
feedback.incorrect: Margins are about profitability, not debt burden.

evidenceRequired: Selects a ratio family based on the business question.
Explains why a ratio is a clue rather than a final answer.

items.prompt: Which ratio family is most directly about profitability from sales: liquidity, leverage, or margin?
hints: Ask how much of sales remains after costs.

feedback.correct: Correct. Margin ratios summarize profitability relative to revenue.
feedback.incorrect: Liquidity asks about paying obligations, not profit from sales.

misconceptions.description: Learner treats ratios as automatic grades instead of question-specific evidence.

remediation.message: Start with the question, then choose the ratio that gives relevant evidence.

concepts.title: Earnings Quality
concepts.summary: Earnings quality asks whether reported profit is repeatable, cash-supported, and free from misleading timing or estimates.
objectives: Identify common earnings-quality warning signs in plain-language scenarios.

diagnostics.prompt: A company reports strong profit but operating cash flow is repeatedly negative. Is the main concern liquidity, earnings quality, or payroll tax?

practice.prompt: A company boosts profit by capitalizing ordinary repairs as assets. Is the concern earnings quality or dividend policy?
hints: Ask whether expenses are being delayed to make profit look better.

feedback.correct: Correct. Misclassifying expenses can make earnings look stronger than they are.
feedback.incorrect: This is about expense timing and classification, not owner distributions.

evidenceRequired: Connects accounting choices to reported profit quality.

items.prompt: A one-time asset sale creates most of the year's profit. Is the concern repeatability or current ratio?
hints: Ask whether the profit source is likely to happen again.

feedback.correct: Correct. One-time gains may not repeat.
feedback.incorrect: Current ratio is about liquidity, not whether earnings recur.

misconceptions.description: Learner assumes reported profit alone proves business health.

remediation.message: Compare profit with cash flow, repeatability, and accounting estimates.

sourceReferences.title: Curriculum scope
sourceReferences.note: Earnings quality is core to Accounting 301.

concepts.title: Unit Economics And Break-Even
concepts.summary: Contribution margin and break-even thinking connect accounting records to operating decisions.
objectives: Identify the key input needed to compute break-even volume.

diagnostics.prompt: Break-even volume equals fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit. If price is $20 and variable cost is $12, what is contribution margin per unit?

practice.prompt: If fixed costs are $1,000 and contribution margin per unit is $10, what is break-even volume?
hints: Divide fixed costs by contribution margin per unit.

feedback.incorrect: Use fixed costs divided by contribution margin per unit.

evidenceRequired: Uses contribution margin to reason about break-even.

items.prompt: Price is $50 and variable cost is $35. What is contribution margin per unit?

feedback.correct: Correct. Each unit contributes $15 toward fixed costs and profit.
feedback.incorrect: Variable cost is not contribution margin; subtract it from price.

misconceptions.description: Learner treats the selling price as contribution margin.

remediation.message: Contribution margin is what remains after variable cost, not the full selling price.

sourceReferences.title: Curriculum scope
sourceReferences.note: Unit economics and managerial accounting are part of Accounting 301.
